intro: The lamp is a hydrogen discharge tube. Its lines $\hbar\omega=13.6\,\mathrm{eV}\,(n^{-2}-n'^{-2})$ come from the Coulomb spectrum $E_n=-e^2/2an^2$ with the unusual degeneracy $n^2$, which is explained by a hidden so(4) symmetry. Perturb the lamp with a magnetic field and the lines split: weak field (anomalous Zeeman, Lande $g$) or strong field (Paschen-Back). The exam routine: write the radial equation, know $\langle r^{k}\rangle$, count states with $n^2$, and use $\vec L\cdot\vec S=\frac12(J^2-L^2-S^2)$.

tutorial.title: The lamp
tutorial.html: The horizontal lines are the levels $E_n=-13.6\,\mathrm{eV}/n^2$ crowding together towards the ionisation threshold $E=0$. The arrows are the emitted photons: Lyman ($n'\to1$), Balmer ($n'\to2$). The orange sphere is an electron in the radial orbit around the proton.

tutorial.title: The Zeeman ladder
tutorial.html: On the left the $2p$ level splits first by spin-orbit coupling ($j=\frac32,\frac12$) and then by $B$ in $2j+1$ equidistant sublevels $g_{lj}\mu_BBm_j$ (weak field). The slope differs between $j=\frac32$ ($g=\frac43$) and $j=\frac12$ ($g=\frac23$).

encounters.title: Why n^2? The hidden so(4) symmetry of the Coulomb problem

blocks.html: Classically the Kepler orbit is closed because of an extra conserved vector, the Runge-Lenz (Pauli-Lenz) vector. Quantum mechanically, for $H=\frac{p^2}{2m}-\frac\kappa r$:

blocks.tex: \vec J=\frac1{2m}\big(\vec p\wedge\vec L-\vec L\wedge\vec p\big)-\kappa\frac{\vec x}{r},\quad [H,\vec J]=0,\quad \vec J\cdot\vec L=0,\quad \vec J^{\,2}=\frac{2H}{m}(\vec L^2+\hbar^2)+\kappa^2
blocks.label: sheet 11 Q1 (1)

blocks.html: On a subspace of fixed $E<0$ the operator $H$ is a number, so $[J_i,J_j]=i\hbar\epsilon_{ijk}\big(-\tfrac{2E}m\big)L_k$ and $[L_i,J_j]=i\hbar\epsilon_{ijk}J_k$. Rescale $\vec J\to a\vec J$ with $a=\sqrt{-m/2E}$ to get the same algebra as $\vec L$. Then $\vec S=\frac12(\vec L+a\vec J)$ and $\vec D=\frac12(\vec L-a\vec J)$ are two commuting su(2) algebras: so(4) $\cong$ su(2)$\oplus$su(2).

blocks.label: uses J.L = 0 (cross terms vanish) and J^2 above

blocks.html: The energy eigenspace is the representation $D_s\otimes D_s$ of dimension $(2s+1)^2=n^2$. Angular momentum is $\vec L=\vec S+\vec D$, so by Clebsch-Gordan $D_s\otimes D_s=\bigoplus_{l=0}^{2s}D_l$ with $l=0,\dots,n-1$ each once: exactly the hydrogen spectrum. The highest-weight state (annihilated by $S_+$ and $D_+$, hence by $L_+$ and $J_+$) is $|n,n-1,n-1\rangle$, with $\psi\propto r^{n-1}\sin^{n-1}\theta\,e^{i(n-1)\phi}e^{-r/(na)}$ (sheet 11 Q1(iii)); lower states come from applying $S_-,D_-$.

The accidental degeneracy in $l$ is thus a true symmetry. A perturbation that is rotation invariant but not so(4) invariant (the $p^4$ correction, the $1/r^2$-type fine structure) lifts it, as seen in the perturbation forge.

blocks.tex: \text{HS22 A.7: }N\text{ commuting su(2) with }\vec A^{(m)2}=\tfrac{15}4\hbar^2\ (s=\tfrac32):\ \ \#\text{states}=(2s+1)^N=4^N,\ N=2\ (n=4)\Rightarrow16=n^2
blocks.label: the hint of the exam: N = 2 is the hydrogen atom

blocks.html: $s=(n-1)/2$ and not $n/2$: $n=1$ must give the trivial representation ($s=0$), one state. And $S^2=D^2$ always, since $\vec L\cdot\vec J=0$.

Symmetries (ii)-(iii). Parity $P\psi(\vec x)=\psi(-\vec x)$: $P\psi=\psi$. Rotations $e^{-i\theta\hat n\cdot\vec L/\hbar}$ with $L_j\psi=0$ because $\psi$ depends only on $r$. If $Q=Q^\dagger$ has $Q\psi=q\psi$, then $\langle[Q,O]\rangle=0$ for any $O$. Parity with $O=x_i$ ($Px_iP=-x_i$, so $\{P,x_i\}=0$) gives $\langle x_i\rangle=0$. With $O=x_k$, $Q=L_j$: $[L_j,x_k]=i\hbar\epsilon_{jkl}x_l$ implies $\langle x_l\rangle=0$ again; with $O=x_kx_l$ one finds $\langle x_ix_j\rangle\propto\delta_{ij}$, so $\langle x_i^2\rangle=\frac13\langle r^2\rangle$.

blocks.html: (v) Sudden change $Z\to\tilde Z$. The wave function does not change during the sudden jump; afterwards the energy is measured. The probability to find the new ground state is the squared overlap with $\tilde\psi=\frac1{\sqrt{\pi\tilde a^3}}e^{-r/\tilde a}$, $\tilde a=a_0/\tilde Z$:

blocks.tex: \langle\tilde\psi|\psi\rangle=\frac{8(a\tilde a)^{3/2}}{(a+\tilde a)^3}=\frac{8(Z\tilde Z)^{3/2}}{(Z+\tilde Z)^3},\qquad P=\frac{64\,(Z\tilde Z)^3}{(Z+\tilde Z)^6}\ \ (Z=1\to2:\ 0.702)
blocks.label: int e^{-beta r} d^3x = 8 pi / beta^3

blocks.html: $P=1$ for $\tilde Z=Z$ and decreases as the two functions differ more. The rest of the probability is shared among excited s-states of the new atom (and the continuum).

Variational principle. For any normalised trial $\phi$: $\langle\phi|H|\phi\rangle\ge E_0$. With $\phi_b\propto e^{-r/b}$: $\langle T\rangle=\frac{\hbar^2}{2mb^2}$, $\langle V\rangle=-\frac{e^2}b$, minimised at $b=a$ with the exact $E=-\frac{e^2}{2a}$, because the trial family contains the exact ground state.
Sign and factor: $\nabla^2$ of $e^{-r/a}$ gives $+\frac1{a^2}-\frac2{ar}$. Forgetting the $\frac2r\partial_r$ term gives no cancellation of the $1/r$ terms and the wrong $a$.

encounters.title: Spin-orbit coupling and the Zeeman effect: strong and weak field

blocks.html: The electron has spin $\vec S$ and moves in the field $V=-e^2/r$: in its rest frame it sees a magnetic field, so $H_{SO}=\frac1{2m^2c^2}\frac1r\frac{dV}{dr}\,\vec L\cdot\vec S=\frac{e^2}{2m^2c^2r^3}\vec L\cdot\vec S$. In a field $B\hat z$: $H_Z=\frac{\mu_BB}{\hbar}(L_z+2S_z)$, $\mu_B=\frac{e\hbar}{2mc}$ (orbital $g=1$, spin $g=2$). Total: $\Delta H=H_{SO}+H_Z$ (sheet 14 Q3).

Zero field. Couple $\vec J=\vec L+\vec S$: $[H_{SO},J^2]=[H_{SO},J_z]=0$, so use $|n,l,j,m_j\rangle$ and $\vec L\cdot\vec S=\frac12(J^2-L^2-S^2)=\frac{\hbar^2}2\big[j(j+1)-l(l+1)-\tfrac34\big]$. With $\langle r^{-3}\rangle=\frac{1}{n^3a^3\,l(l+\frac12)(l+1)}$:

Strong field (Paschen-Back, (i)): $\mu_BB\gg E^{SO}$, treat $H_{SO}$ as a perturbation of $H_0+H_Z$. The good basis is $|n,l,m_l,m_s\rangle$ with $E=\mu_BB(m_l+2m_s)$, and $\langle\vec L\cdot\vec S\rangle=\hbar^2m_lm_s$ (only $L_zS_z$ is diagonal):
Weak field (anomalous Zeeman, (iii)): $H_Z$ is the perturbation in the $j$-basis. The projection theorem (Wigner-Eckart) gives $\langle jm_j|L_z+2S_z|jm_j\rangle=g_{lj}\,\hbar m_j$ with

Weak field: the field only splits each $j$ multiplet ($2j+1$ equidistant levels, spacing $g\mu_BB$), so there are more lines than the "normal" Zeeman triplet. Strong field: the spin-orbit term is a small correction to the free Larmor levels $\mu_BB(m_l+2m_s)$ and the "normal" triplet returns. Intermediate fields need the $2\times2$ blocks of the sheet hint (block diagonal because $[L^2,\Delta H]=[L_z+S_z,\Delta H]=0$).

The factor 2 in front of $S_z$ is the electron's spin $g$-factor, it is why $g_{lj}\neq1$. For $l=0$ there is no spin-orbit coupling and $g=2$. Do not mix $j$ and $l$: $m_j$ runs over $2j+1$ values, not $2l+1$.

encounters.title: Radial equation: boundary behaviour and quantisation of $E_n$

source.where: Ch. 8.2, pp. 84-87; method of sheet 10 Q1 (ii)-(iv)

encounters.goal: Show $u\sim r^{l+1}$ and $u\sim e^{-\sqrt{-2mE}r/\hbar}$, and that termination of the power series gives $E_n=-e^2/(2an^2)$.

steps.reveal: Dominant terms: $-u''+\frac{l(l+1)}{r^2}u=0$. Try $u=r^s$: $s(s-1)=l(l+1)$, so $s=l+1$ or $s=-l$. The second makes $\Psi=\frac urY$ singular like $r^{-l-1}$ and not a solution at the origin (for $l=0$ a delta function), so $u\sim r^{l+1}$.

steps.prompt: (b) Behaviour at large $r$ and the ansatz.
steps.reveal: For $r\to\infty$: $u''=\kappa^2u$ with $\kappa=\sqrt{-2mE}/\hbar$ (needs $E<0$), $u\sim e^{-\kappa r}$. Ansatz: $u=e^{-\kappa r}\sum_{k\ge l+1}c_kr^k$.

steps.prompt: (c) Insert into the equation and find the recursion.
steps.reveal: Collecting $r^{k-1}$: $\big[k(k+1)-l(l+1)\big]c_{k+1}=\big[2\kappa k-\frac{2me^2}{\hbar^2}\big]c_k$, i.e. $c_{k+1}=\frac{2(\kappa k-1/a)}{k(k+1)-l(l+1)}c_k$ with $a=\hbar^2/me^2$.

If it does not, $c_{k+1}/c_k\to2\kappa/k$ and the series behaves like $e^{2\kappa r}$, so $u\sim e^{+\kappa r}$ and the state is not normalisable. Termination at $k_{max}$ requires $\kappa k_{max}=1/a$.

$\kappa=1/(na)$ with $n=k_{max}\ge l+1$ integer, hence $E=-\frac{\hbar^2\kappa^2}{2m}=-\frac{\hbar^2}{2ma^2n^2}=-\frac{e^2}{2an^2}$; $l\le n-1$ gives $\sum(2l+1)=n^2$. For the oscillator the large-$r$ behaviour is $e^{-m\omega r^2/2\hbar}$ and the energies are $\hbar\omega(2k+l+\frac32)$ (sheet 10 Q1).

keyPoints: recursion for the coefficients and termination condition $\kappa k_{max}=1/a$

encounters.title: Ground state of a hydrogenic atom (HS25 Q2 (i))
encounters.goal: Show that $\psi=\frac1{\sqrt{\pi a^3}}e^{-r/a}$ solves $H\psi=E\psi$ for a certain $a$; find $a$ and $E$.
given: $\nabla^2\psi=\psi''+\frac2r\psi'$ for radial functions (the angular terms of the given Laplacian vanish)

steps.reveal: $\psi'=-\psi/a$, $\psi''=\psi/a^2$, so $\nabla^2\psi=\big(\frac1{a^2}-\frac2{ar}\big)\psi$.
$H\psi=-\frac{\hbar^2}{2m}\big(\frac1{a^2}-\frac2{ar}\big)\psi-\frac{Ze^2}r\psi=\Big[-\frac{\hbar^2}{2ma^2}+\Big(\frac{\hbar^2}{ma}-Ze^2\Big)\frac1r\Big]\psi$.

steps.prompt: (c) Demand an eigenfunction and read off $a$.
steps.reveal: The $1/r$ term must vanish: $a=\frac{\hbar^2}{mZe^2}=\frac{a_0}Z$.
$E=-\frac{\hbar^2}{2ma^2}=-\frac{Z^2e^2}{2a_0}=-Z^2\cdot13.6$ eV. Normalisation: $\int|\psi|^2d^3x=\frac{4\pi}{\pi a^3}\int r^2e^{-2r/a}dr=\frac4{a^3}\cdot2\Big(\frac a2\Big)^3=1$.

encounters.title: Symmetry constraints and uncertainty for the ground state (HS25 Q2 (ii)-(iv))
encounters.goal: Show $\langle x_i\rangle=0$, $\langle x_i^2\rangle=\frac13\langle r^2\rangle$, evaluate $\Delta x_i$ and check $\Delta x_i\Delta p_j\ge\hbar/2$.
given: $\psi=\frac1{\sqrt{\pi a^3}}e^{-r/a}$, parity $P\psi(\vec x)=\psi(-\vec x)$, rotations $R=e^{-i\theta\hat n\cdot\vec L/\hbar}$

steps.prompt: (a) How do the symmetries act on $\psi$?
steps.reveal: $P\psi=\psi$ (eigenvalue $+1$, $\psi$ is even); $L_j\psi=0$ since $\psi=\psi(r)$ has no angular dependence, so $R\psi=\psi$.

$\langle\psi|[Q,O]\psi\rangle=\langle Q\psi|O\psi\rangle-\langle\psi|OQ\psi\rangle=(q-q)\langle O\rangle=0$ for hermitian $Q$. With $Q=L_j$: $0=\langle[L_j,x_k]\rangle=i\hbar\epsilon_{jkl}\langle x_l\rangle$, so all $\langle x_l\rangle=0$.

With $O=x_kx_m$ the same relation gives $\epsilon_{jkl}\langle x_lx_m\rangle+\epsilon_{jml}\langle x_kx_l\rangle=0$, which forces $\langle x_ix_j\rangle=c\,\delta_{ij}$; the trace gives $3c=\langle r^2\rangle$. (Alternatively: symmetry of $|\psi|^2$ under rotation.)

$\langle r^2\rangle=\frac4{a^3}\int r^4e^{-2r/a}dr=\frac4{a^3}\cdot24\frac{a^5}{32}=3a^2$, so $\Delta x_i=a$. Then $\Delta x_i\Delta p_j=\frac{\hbar}{\sqrt3}\approx0.577\hbar\ge\frac\hbar2$: satisfied.

encounters.title: so(4): $S^2=D^2$ and the $n^2$ degeneracy (sheet 11 Q1)
encounters.goal: Show that at energy $E_n$ the algebra su(2)$\oplus$su(2) acts as $D_s\otimes D_s$ with $s=\frac{n-1}2$ and that this contains exactly $l=0,\dots,n-1$.
given: $\vec S=\frac12(\vec L+a\vec J)$, $\vec D=\frac12(\vec L-a\vec J)$, $a=\sqrt{-m/2E}$

steps.reveal: $a^2[J_i,J_j]=a^2(-\frac{2E}m)i\hbar\epsilon_{ijk}L_k=i\hbar\epsilon_{ijk}L_k$ at fixed $E$; with $[L_i,J_j]=i\hbar\epsilon_{ijk}J_k$ both $\vec S$, $\vec D$ close, and the cross commutator $\frac14([L,L]-a^2[J,J]\mp\dots)$ cancels.
$S^2=\frac14\big(L^2+a^2J^2+2a\vec L\cdot\vec J\big)=\frac14\big(L^2+a^2\tfrac{2E}m(L^2+\hbar^2)+a^2\kappa^2\big)$. With $a^2\frac{2E}m=-1$: $S^2=\frac14\big(-\hbar^2-\frac{m\kappa^2}{2E}\big)=D^2$.
$E_n=-\frac{m\kappa^2}{2\hbar^2n^2}$ gives $-\frac{m\kappa^2}{2E}=\hbar^2n^2$, so $S^2=D^2=\frac{\hbar^2}{4}(n^2-1)=\hbar^2s(s+1)$ with $s=\frac{n-1}2$.
$D_s\otimes D_s=\bigoplus_{l=0}^{2s}D_l$ with $2s=n-1$: dimension $(2s+1)^2=n^2$. The highest weight $|s,s\rangle\otimes|s,s\rangle$ has $L_z=2s\hbar=(n-1)\hbar$, $l=n-1$: it is $|n,n-1,n-1\rangle$.

encounters.title: Landé $g$-factor and the Paschen-Back limit (sheet 14 Q3 (i), (iii))
encounters.goal: Show $\Delta E=g_{lj}\mu_BBm_j$ with $g_{l,l+1/2}=\frac{2+2l}{1+2l}$ and give the Paschen-Back energies.

steps.prompt: (a) Rewrite $L_z+2S_z$ and use the projection theorem.
steps.reveal: $L_z+2S_z=J_z+S_z$. Within a $j$ multiplet $\vec S\to\frac{\langle\vec S\cdot\vec J\rangle}{j(j+1)\hbar^2}\vec J$, so $\langle S_z\rangle=\frac{\langle\vec S\cdot\vec J\rangle}{j(j+1)\hbar^2}\hbar m_j$.
$\vec S\cdot\vec J=\frac{\hbar^2}2\big[j(j+1)+\frac34-l(l+1)\big]$. Hence $g=1+\frac{j(j+1)+\frac34-l(l+1)}{2j(j+1)}$.

$j=l+\frac12$: $j(j+1)=l^2+2l+\frac34$, so the numerator is $l+\frac32$ and $g=1+\frac{l+3/2}{(2l+1)(l+3/2)}=\frac{2l+2}{2l+1}$ (check $l=1$: $\frac43$). $j=l-\frac12$: $j(j+1)=l^2-\frac14$, numerator $\frac12-l$, $g=1-\frac1{2l+1}=\frac{2l}{2l+1}$ (check $l=1$: $\frac23$).

$H_Z$ dominates: eigenstates $|m_l,m_s\rangle$, $E=\mu_BB(m_l+2m_s)$; first-order spin-orbit with $\langle\vec L\cdot\vec S\rangle=\hbar^2m_lm_s$ and $\langle r^{-3}\rangle=\frac1{n^3a^3l(l+\frac12)(l+1)}$. Valid for $\mu_BB\gg$ the spin-orbit splitting ($\gtrsim 0.8$ T for $2p$).

encounters.title: Variational principle for the hydrogen ground state

source.where: variational principle (supplementary; not in the lecturer script)

encounters.goal: Show $\langle\phi|H|\phi\rangle\ge E_0$ for every normalised $\phi$ and apply it to $\phi_b\propto e^{-r/b}$.

steps.prompt: (a) Expand $\phi=\sum c_n|n\rangle$ and show the bound.
steps.reveal: $\langle H\rangle=\sum|c_n|^2E_n\ge E_0\sum|c_n|^2=E_0$.
$\langle T\rangle=\frac{\hbar^2}{2m}\langle\nabla\phi|\nabla\phi\rangle=\frac{\hbar^2}{2mb^2}$ (as $\langle p^2\rangle=\hbar^2/b^2$), $\langle V\rangle=-e^2\langle1/r\rangle=-\frac{e^2}b$.
$\frac d{db}\big(\frac{\hbar^2}{2mb^2}-\frac{e^2}b\big)=-\frac{\hbar^2}{mb^3}+\frac{e^2}{b^2}=0\Rightarrow b=\frac{\hbar^2}{me^2}=a$, $E_{min}=-\frac{e^2}{2a}$.

steps.prompt: (d) Why is the answer exact here?
steps.reveal: The trial family contains the true ground state $e^{-r/a}$. For a Gaussian trial function the minimum would be $-\frac{4}{3\pi}\frac{e^2}{a}=-0.424\frac{e^2}{a}>-0.5\frac{e^2}a$: still above $E_0$.

encounters.title: Sudden change of the nuclear charge (HS25 Q2 (v))
encounters.problem: A hydrogenic atom with charge $Ze$ is in its ground state. The nuclear charge suddenly becomes $\tilde Ze$ and the energy is measured at once. Find the probability of the new ground-state energy. Source: HS25 Q2 (v).
symbols: ground states of the old and new Hamiltonian

derivation.title: Method
derivation.html: Sudden approximation: the state is unchanged right after the jump, $\psi$; the energy measurement projects on eigenstates of the new $H$. So $P=|\langle\tilde\psi|\psi\rangle|^2$ with $\int e^{-\beta r}d^3x=8\pi/\beta^3$.

steps.prompt: What is the state immediately after the jump?
options: still $\psi=\frac1{\sqrt{\pi a^3}}e^{-r/a}$: a sudden change leaves the wave function unchanged
a superposition fixed by the energy change

why.0: That would be an adiabatic (slow) change.
why.1: Normalisation does not change; $\psi$ is simply continuous in time.
why.3: The state is determined by continuity; the superposition appears when you expand it in the new eigenstates.

why.2: That is an average energy ratio, not the probability.

encounters.problem: Compute the spin-orbit splitting between $2p_{3/2}$ and $2p_{1/2}$ in hydrogen, using $H_{SO}=\frac{e^2}{2m^2c^2r^3}\vec L\cdot\vec S$ and $\langle r^{-3}\rangle_{nl}=\frac1{n^3a^3l(l+\frac12)(l+1)}$. Source: sheet 14 Q3 (ii)-(iii), script eq. (9.7.29).
symbols: total angular momentum $\vec J=\vec L+\vec S$

derivation.title: Method
derivation.html: $H_{SO}$ commutes with $J^2,J_z,L^2$ so the $|l,s;j,m_j\rangle$ basis diagonalises it; use $\vec L\cdot\vec S=\frac12(J^2-L^2-S^2)$ and $e^2\hbar^2/(m a)=e^4$.

options: any basis, since $H_{SO}$ is a scalar

why.1: $L_+S_-$ terms connect different $(m_l,m_s)$ with the same $m_j$.
why.3: Scalar under total $J$, not diagonal in the uncoupled basis.

steps.prompt: Which of the two levels lies lower, and by what ratio?
options: $2p_{1/2}$ lies lower; the shifts are in ratio $+\frac1{96}:-\frac1{48}$, i.e. the centre of gravity $(4\cdot\frac1{96}+2\cdot(-\frac1{48}))=0$ is preserved

why.0: The sign of $\vec L\cdot\vec S$ is positive for parallel $\vec L,\vec S$ ($j=l+\frac12$) and $e^2/r^3>0$: that level is higher.
why.1: The trace of $\vec L\cdot\vec S$ over the 6 states vanishes.

steps.prompt: Bonus: the splitting $E(2p_{3/2})-E(2p_{1/2})$ in eV (alpha, mc2 in eV).

encounters.title: Zeeman splitting of $2p$: weak or strong field? (sheet 14 Q3)
encounters.problem: The $2p$ level of hydrogen sits in a field $B\hat z$. Decide which limit applies, compute the $g$-factors and the shifts, and the field strength at which $\mu_BB$ equals the spin-orbit splitting. Source: sheet 14 Q3.

options: neither: $\mu_BB\ll$ the Bohr energy, so nothing happens
weak field: $\mu_BB=5.8\times10^{-7}$ eV $\ll\Delta E^{SO}$, so use the $j$ basis and $g_{lj}\mu_BBm_j$
the field is too weak to split anything

why.0: That needs $\mu_BB\gg\Delta E^{SO}\approx4.5\times10^{-5}$ eV, i.e. $B\gg0.8$ T.
why.1: The relevant comparison is with the fine-structure splitting, not with $E_n$.
why.3: It splits each $j$ multiplet; a small but non-zero splitting.

steps.prompt: Order the steps of the weak-field derivation.

items.why: First rewriting: it exposes the part proportional to $J_z$.

items.text: Replace $\vec S$ in the $j$ multiplet by its projection on $\vec J$
items.why: Needs the rewriting so that only $\vec S$ remains to be projected.
Needs the projection factor to be known.

steps.prompt: Bonus: the field in tesla at which $\mu_BB=\alpha^4mc^2/32$ (muB in eV/T).

encounters.title: Ground state of a hydrogenic atom (HS25 Q2)

source.where: Question 2 [Ground state of a hydrogenic atom, 20 points]

encounters.instructions: Solve on paper under the timer (2 min per point). Then enter the numbers.
statement: Consider the Hamiltonian of an electron orbiting a nucleus of charge $Ze$, $H=-\frac{\hbar^2}{2m}\nabla^2-\frac{Ze^2}r$, $r=\sqrt{\vec x^2}$.

(i) Show that the (normalised) ground state wave function $\psi(\vec x)=\frac1{\sqrt{\pi a^3}}e^{-r/a}$ is an eigenfunction of $H$ for a certain value of $a$. Determine $a$ and the eigenvalue $E$ in terms of $Z$. [4 points] Hint: The Laplacian in spherical coordinates $(r,\theta,\phi)$ is $\nabla^2=\partial_r^2+\frac2r\partial_r+\frac1{r^2}\partial_\theta^2+\frac{\cot\theta}{r^2}\partial_\theta+\frac1{r^2\sin^2\theta}\partial_\phi^2$.

(ii) The Hamiltonian has a parity symmetry $P$, and a rotational symmetry generated by $L_j$, $j=1,2,3$. Define how these symmetries act on wavefunctions, and evaluate them on $\psi$ from eq. (10). [4 points]

(iii) Show that the symmetries from (ii) imply that $\langle x_i\rangle=0$, $\langle x_i^2\rangle=\frac13\langle\vec x^2\rangle$, where $\langle O\rangle:=\langle\psi|O|\psi\rangle$. [4 points] Hint: Let $Q=Q^\dagger$ be a self-adjoint (symmetry) generator, for which $\psi$ is an eigenstate. What can you say about $\langle[Q,O]\rangle$? You may also use the commutation relations $[L_j,x_k]=i\hbar\varepsilon_{jkl}x_l$.

(iv) Calculate the variation $\Delta x_i$. Use the variation $\Delta p_j=\frac{\hbar}{\sqrt3a}$ to show that the Heisenberg uncertainty principle is satisfied. [4 points] Hint: The following integral may be helpful, $\int_0^\infty dr\,r^ne^{-r/b}=b^{n+1}n!$.

(v) The system is in the state $\psi$ in eq. (10). Then, the charge of the nucleus is suddenly changed to $\tilde Ze$, and the energy is measured immediately afterwards. What is the probability that the ground state energy of the new system is measured? [4 points]
keyPoints: (ii) $P\psi(\vec x)=\psi(-\vec x)=\psi$; rotations act by $e^{-i\vec\theta\cdot\vec L/\hbar}$, $L_j\psi=0$ since $\psi=\psi(r)$

(iii) $\langle[Q,O]\rangle=0$ for an eigenstate of $Q$; parity with $O=x_i$ and $L_j$ with $[L_j,x_k]=i\hbar\epsilon_{jkl}x_l$ give $\langle x_i\rangle=0$, $\langle x_ix_j\rangle\propto\delta_{ij}$, so $\langle x_i^2\rangle=\frac13\langle r^2\rangle$

encounters.title: The dynamical symmetry of hydrogen (sheet 11 Q1 with HS22 A.7)

source.where: Question 1 [More on the dynamical symmetry]; with HS22 A.7 as the counting check

encounters.instructions: Sheet problem used as a boss (exam-style, the algebraic route to the hydrogen spectrum). Solve on paper under the timer, then enter the numbers.
statement: The additional conserved charge for the hydrogen atom $H=\frac{p^2}{2m}-\frac\kappa r$ is the Pauli-Lenz vector $\vec J=\frac1{2m}(\vec p\wedge\vec L-\vec L\wedge\vec p)-\kappa\frac{\vec x}r$. On a subspace of fixed negative energy, one can form an su(2)$\oplus$su(2) algebra by combining $\vec S=\frac12(\vec L+a\vec J)$, $\vec D=\frac12(\vec L-a\vec J)$, with $a$ some energy dependent factor. We want to describe the representations of this algebra which appear for the hydrogen atom more concretely.

(i) We know that the eigenspace of energy $E_n$ is spanned by $|n,l,m\rangle$, $l=0,\dots,n-1$, $m=-l,\dots,l$. In this space, there must exist a highest weight vector $|\psi\rangle$ which is annihilated by $S_+$ and $D_+$. Show that this vector must satisfy $J_+|\psi\rangle=L_+|\psi\rangle=0$, and that therefore $|\psi\rangle$ must be a superposition of $|n,l,l\rangle$, $l=0,\dots,n-1$.

(ii) Calculate the commutators $[L_\pm,J_+]$, $[L_3,J_+]$, and use the result to show that $J_+|n,l,l\rangle\propto|n,l+1,l+1\rangle$. Conclude that the highest weight vector is given by $|\psi\rangle=|n,n-1,n-1\rangle$. Hint: Use the commutation relations $[L_j,J_k]=i\hbar\varepsilon_{jkl}J_l$ and the definition $V_\pm=V_1\pm iV_2$.

(iii) For the argument in the previous section, we needed to know the bound $l\le n-1$. We now want to show these properties by explicit calculation. (a) First, use the method from Section 8.2.2 in the lecture notes to show that the wavefunction of $|n,n-1,n-1\rangle$ is given by $\psi(r,\theta,\phi)\propto r^{n-1}\sin^{n-1}\theta\,e^{i(n-1)\phi}\exp\big(-\frac{m\kappa}{\hbar^2n}r\big)$. (b) Show that $J_+$ can be expressed as $J_+=\frac im\big(p_3L_+-\hbar p_+-p_+L_3\big)-\kappa\sin\theta\,e^{i\phi}$. (c) Show that $J_+\psi(r,\theta,\phi)=0$.

(v) Use the results from the previous exercises to give a description of the energy eigenspace in terms of ladder operators acting on $|n,n-1,n-1\rangle$. Once more count the degeneracy of this eigenspace.

Counting check (HS22 A.7): $N=2$ vector operators $\vec A^{(m)}$ obeying $[A_i^{(m)},A_j^{(n)}]=i\hbar\epsilon_{ijk}A_k^{(m)}\delta_{mn}$ with $\vec A^{(m)2}=\frac{15}4\hbar^2$ for all $m$: how many degenerate states are simultaneous eigenstates of $\vec A^{(m)2}$ and $A_3^{(m)}$?

finalAnswers.prompt: The spin $s$ of both su(2) factors for $n=3$.

keyPoints: (i) $S_+\psi=D_+\psi=0$: add and subtract, $L_+\psi=0$ and $aJ_+\psi=0$; $L_+\psi=0$ means $\psi$ is a superposition of $m=l$ states $|n,l,l\rangle$
(ii) $[L_3,J_+]=\hbar J_+$, $[L_+,J_+]=0$, $[L_-,J_+]=2\hbar J_3$: $J_+$ raises $l$ and $m$ together, and it must annihilate the state, which is only possible at $l=n-1$
(iii) $L_+\psi=0$ and $L^2\psi=\hbar^2(n-1)n\psi$ give the angular dependence $\sin^{n-1}\theta e^{i(n-1)\phi}$; the radial part follows from the radial equation ($u\sim r^ne^{-r/na}$)
(v) $S^2=D^2=\hbar^2\frac{n^2-1}4$: apply $S_-$ and $D_-$ up to $2s=n-1$ times each; $n^2$ states

encounters.title: Spin-orbit coupling and the Zeeman effect (sheet 14 Q3)

source.where: Question 3 [Spin-orbit coupling and Zeeman effect]; solution Solutions 14

encounters.instructions: Sheet problem used as a boss (the standard exam topic "fine structure in a magnetic field", compare HS16 1.3). Solve on paper under the timer, then enter the numbers.
statement: Consider an electron in a hydrogen atom in the presence of a constant magnetic field $\vec B$, which we take to be parallel to the $z$-axis. Without the magnetic field and ignoring the spin-orbit coupling, the eigenfunctions are labelled by $(n,\ell,m,m_s)$, where $m_s$ denotes the spin quantum number $m_s=\pm\frac12$. The additional effects lead to $H=H_0+\Delta H$ with $\Delta H=H_{SO}+H_Z=\frac1{2m_e^2c^2}\frac1r\frac{dV}{dr}\vec L\cdot\vec S+\frac{\mu_BB_z}{\hbar}(L_z+2S_z)$, where $V(r)=-e^2/r$ and $\mu_B=\frac{e\hbar}{2m_ec}$ is the Bohr magneton.

(i) If the second term dominates (Paschen-Back effect), determine the first order perturbation of the energy spectrum, treating only the spin-orbit coupling as a perturbation. How big does $B_z$ have to be in order to justify this approximation? Hint: $\langle\frac1{r^3}\rangle_{n\ell}=\frac1{a_0^3}\frac1{n^3\ell(\ell+1/2)(\ell+1)}$, where $a_0:=\hbar^2/(m_ee^2)$ is the Bohr radius.

(ii) Next, determine the energy spectrum to first order perturbation theory, treating both terms (i.e. $\Delta H$) as a perturbation. Hint: You need to diagonalise the $2n^2\times2n^2$ matrix where $\ell=0,1,\dots,n-1$, $m=-\ell,\dots,\ell$ and $m_s=\pm\frac12$. Since $[\vec L^2,\Delta H]=[L_z+S_z,\Delta H]=0$, this matrix is block-diagonal with $2\times2$ blocks.

(iii) For $B_z=0$, reproduce the result for the spin orbit coupling that was derived in the lectures. Show that the first order correction in $B_z$ of this result is given by $\Delta E_{n\ell jm_j}=g_{\ell j}\mu_BB_zm_j$, $m_j=-j,\dots,j$, where $j$ and $m_j$ refer to the diagonal representation of the rotation group corresponding to $\vec J=\vec L+\vec S$ and $g_{\ell,\ell+1/2}=\frac{2+2\ell}{1+2\ell}$, $g_{\ell,\ell-1/2}=\frac{2\ell}{1+2\ell}$.

finalAnswers.prompt: (iii) Zeeman shift of $2p_{3/2}$, $m_j=\frac32$ in units of $\mu_BB$.
(ii) Number of $2\times2$ blocks of the $2n^2\times2n^2$ matrix for $n=2$ (the extreme states $m_j=\pm(\ell+\frac12)$ and all $\ell=0$ states are $1\times1$ blocks).

keyPoints: (i) good states $|n,\ell,m_l,m_s\rangle$, $\langle\vec L\cdot\vec S\rangle=\hbar^2m_lm_s$: $E=\mu_BB(m_l+2m_s)+\frac{e^2\hbar^2m_lm_s}{2m^2c^2a_0^3n^3\ell(\ell+\frac12)(\ell+1)}$; requires $\mu_BB\gg$ fine-structure splitting ($B\gg0.8$ T for $n=2$)

(ii) the matrix is conserved in $m_j=m_l+m_s$ and $\ell$: blocks $\{|m_l=m_j-\frac12,\uparrow\rangle,|m_l=m_j+\frac12,\downarrow\rangle\}$; $2\times2$ diagonalisation gives the Breit-Rabi type formula; the extreme states $m_j=\pm(\ell+\frac12)$ are $1\times1$ blocks
